analogy.p: Think of the reacting solution like a flask of tea in a polystyrene cup. A good insulated flask keeps the heat in, so the temperature you measure shows what the tea was really doing. If the flask is a thin glass cup, the tea cools quickly and you read a lower temperature than expected, just as heat loss from an unlit beaker gives a smaller temperature rise. This maps to the insulating cup and lid. It breaks down because in the practical the heat is being produced by the reaction itself, not just stored, and the reaction stops when the reactants are used up.

bullets: **Aim:** to find out how a chosen variable (for example the type of metal, the concentration of the acid or the volume of alkali added) affects the **temperature change** when two reactants are mixed.

**Reaction types you may be given:** acid + metal, acid + carbonate, neutralisation (acid + alkali), and displacement of one metal by a more reactive metal (for example zinc + copper sulfate solution).
**Key measurement:** the temperature of the solution before and after the reaction, so the **temperature change** = final (highest) temperature − starting temperature.

**Skills assessed:** choosing equipment, controlling variables, reading a thermometer, repeating readings, calculating a mean, plotting a graph, drawing lines of best fit, drawing conclusions and suggesting improvements.

**Why it matters:** the temperature change is the evidence that tells you whether a reaction is **exothermic** (temperature rises) or **endothermic** (temperature falls), linking to 4.5.1 energy changes.
**Exam link:** you may be asked to describe the method, name equipment, state a hazard, explain why a lid is used, or interpret a graph or results table from this practical.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know and do
core.p: This is AQA required practical 4: **investigate the variables that affect temperature changes in reacting solutions**, for example acid plus metals, acid plus carbonates, neutralisations and displacement of metals. You must be able to carry out the method safely, measure temperatures accurately, process the results, plot and interpret graphs, and evaluate the investigation. Questions on required practicals test the practical skills themselves (planning, variables, safety, accuracy, graphs, conclusions) as much as the chemistry, and this practical (in the energy changes topic) is examined in Paper 1, although practical skills can be tested on any paper, for both Combined and Separate Science.

bullets: **Exothermic:** energy transferred to the surroundings, temperature of the surroundings **increases** (neutralisation, acid + metal, displacement of copper by zinc).
**Endothermic:** energy taken in from the surroundings, temperature of the surroundings **decreases** (for example citric acid reacting with sodium hydrogencarbonate).
**Energy is conserved:** energy is not created or destroyed, it is only transferred, so the energy lost by the chemicals appears as a temperature rise in the solution.
**Why use the same volume:** the temperature change depends on how much solution there is to heat up, so volume must be kept constant for a fair test.
**What is measured:** the solution is the surroundings of the reacting particles, so its temperature tells you about the energy transfer.
**Link:** this is the practical evidence for the theory in 4.5.1.1 (exothermic and endothermic reactions) and gives context for reaction profiles.
core.h: The scientific idea behind the measurement
core.p: When a reaction happens in a solution, energy is transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings. In an **exothermic** reaction energy is transferred **to** the surroundings, so the solution warms up. In an **endothermic** reaction energy is taken in **from** the surroundings, so the solution cools down. We cannot see energy moving, but we can see its effect on the temperature of the solution, which is why a thermometer is the key piece of equipment. If the same volume of solution is used each time, a bigger temperature change means a bigger energy transfer, which makes comparisons fair.

bullets: **Polystyrene cup:** an insulator, so it reduces energy transfer to or from the surroundings. A glass beaker alone would lose energy faster.
**Beaker (250 cm³):** supports the cup and stops it falling over; the air gap adds extra insulation.
**Lid with a hole for the thermometer:** reduces heat loss by evaporation and convection and keeps spray inside.
**Thermometer or digital probe:** a digital probe reads to 0.1 °C, which has a higher **resolution** than a thermometer marked in 1 °C steps.
**Measuring cylinder:** more accurate than a beaker for measuring volumes; a pipette or burette is more accurate still.
**Stirring rod:** used to mix the reactants so the temperature is the same throughout the solution; do **not** stir with the thermometer because glass can break.
**Balance and spatula (if solids are used):** to measure the same mass of metal or carbonate each time.
**Stopwatch (if a temperature–time graph is plotted):** to take readings at fixed time intervals.
core.h: Equipment and why each piece is used
core.p: The standard apparatus is deliberately simple. A **polystyrene cup** is used as the reaction container because polystyrene is an excellent insulator, so very little energy escapes to the surroundings and the temperature change measured is closer to the true value. The cup is placed inside a **beaker** because the cup is light and tips over easily, and the beaker also adds a layer of trapped air for insulation. A **lid** on the cup further reduces heat loss by convection and evaporation. A **thermometer** (or digital temperature probe) measures the temperature, a **measuring cylinder** measures the volume of solution accurately, and a **balance** is used if a mass of solid is needed.

bullets: **Step 1:** place a polystyrene cup inside a 250 cm³ beaker for support.
**Step 2:** use a measuring cylinder to measure a fixed volume (for example 25 cm³) of the first solution (acid or copper sulfate) and pour it into the cup.
**Step 3:** put the lid on, insert the thermometer and record the **starting temperature** once the reading is steady (T1).
**Step 4:** add the second reagent (a measured mass of metal or carbonate, or a measured volume of alkali), replace the lid quickly and **stir gently**.
**Step 5:** watch the thermometer and record the **highest** temperature reached (T2) for an exothermic reaction (or the lowest for an endothermic one).
**Step 6:** calculate the **temperature change** = T2 − T1.
**Step 7:** rinse and dry the cup, and **repeat** the experiment at least twice more under identical conditions.
**Step 8:** change one variable (for example the metal) and repeat the whole procedure, keeping everything else the same.
**Neutralisation version:** add the alkali in 5 cm³ portions, stir and record the maximum temperature after each portion, until the temperature starts to fall.
core.p: The method is the same for most versions of the practical: measure a fixed volume of one solution into the insulated cup, record its temperature, add the second reactant, stir, and record the highest temperature reached. Because the aim is to measure the energy transferred as the reaction happens, the temperature is read **while stirring**, and the **maximum** (or minimum for an endothermic reaction) temperature is recorded. The whole procedure is repeated so that a mean and any anomalies can be identified. Always write the method in the order of events and include quantities so the experiment could be repeated by someone else.

bullets: **Dependent variable:** the temperature change (°C) of the solution, measured with a thermometer or digital probe.
**Independent variable (example 1):** the **type of metal** added to acid (for example magnesium, zinc, iron).
**Independent variable (example 2):** the **concentration of the acid**, or the **volume of alkali** added in a neutralisation.
**Control variable: volume of solution** (affects how much liquid is heated, so the same volume gives comparable temperature changes).
**Control variable: concentration of the solution** (a more concentrated solution contains more reacting particles, so would release more energy).
**Control variable: mass and form of solid** (for example the same mass of magnesium ribbon of the same length, because powder reacts faster and may lose less heat).
**Control variable: starting temperature** (so every reaction starts from the same temperature and the change is comparable).
**Control variable: the apparatus and stirring** (the same cup and lid, and the same stirring method each time).
**Why control variables matter:** if more than one variable changes, you cannot say which one caused the difference in temperature change, so the conclusion would not be **valid**.
core.p: Every fair test needs one **independent variable** (the one you deliberately change), one **dependent variable** (the one you measure) and a list of **control variables** (everything that must stay the same, otherwise you cannot tell what caused the change). In this practical the dependent variable is nearly always the **temperature change** (or the highest temperature reached). The independent variable depends on the version being investigated. You will often be asked to name a suitable independent variable and at least two control variables, and to explain why each matters.

bullets: **Use a polystyrene cup:** its structure traps air, making it a poor conductor, so less energy transfers through the sides.
**Use a lid:** reduces energy lost by evaporation and convection from the surface of the liquid.
**Place the cup inside a beaker, and a layer of cotton wool or lagging around it** for extra insulation.
**Record the temperature quickly and at the peak:** the maximum is reached and then the solution cools, so read the thermometer continuously.
**Stir the solution:** ensures the thermometer reads the temperature of the whole solution, not just one warm or cool spot.
**Other errors:** thermometer resolution (a 1 °C scale limits precision), human error reading the scale (parallax), incomplete reaction, and not stirring.

**Systematic error:** heat loss always makes an exothermic temperature rise too small, so it is a **systematic** error, not a random one; repeating readings does not remove it, only better insulation does.
**Reading the thermometer:** keep your eye level with the liquid surface and wait for the temperature to stop changing before recording the starting temperature.
core.h: Reducing energy loss and other sources of error
core.p: The biggest source of error in this practical is **heat transfer to or from the surroundings**. In an exothermic reaction, some energy escapes into the air through the sides, the top and by evaporation, so the highest temperature measured is lower than it would be in a perfectly insulated system. In an endothermic reaction, energy enters from the warmer room, so the temperature does not fall as far as it should. Either way, heat exchange with the surroundings makes the measured temperature change smaller than the true value. Good technique and insulation keep this error as small as possible.

bullets: **Resolution:** the smallest division you can read; for a thermometer with 1 °C divisions you can read to the nearest 0.5 °C, which limits the precision of a small temperature change.
**Repeats:** do at least three repeats for each condition; this lets you spot **anomalies** and calculate a **mean**.
**Anomalous result:** one that does not fit the pattern (for example 10.0 °C when the others are 6.5 °C); it is ignored when calculating the mean, and you should say why it might have happened.
**Mean = sum of valid results ÷ number of valid results** (leave out anomalies).
**Repeatable:** same operator, same equipment, results agree closely. **Reproducible:** different operator or equipment, results still agree.
**Precision vs accuracy:** precise results are close together; accurate results are close to the true value. Systematic errors reduce accuracy but not precision.
**Record to a consistent number of decimal places** (for example one decimal place for a thermometer reading to 0.5 °C or 0.1 °C).
**Table layout:** put the independent variable in the first column, include units in column headings (not in the table body), and add columns for each repeat, the mean and the temperature change.
core.h: Taking readings: resolution, repeats and anomalies
core.p: A measurement is only useful if it is **precise** (small spread) and **accurate** (close to the true value). **Resolution** is the smallest change a measuring instrument can detect; a digital probe reading to 0.1 °C gives a smaller uncertainty than a thermometer marked every 1 °C. To improve reliability, the experiment is **repeated** and a **mean** is calculated. Results are **repeatable** if the same person gets similar results using the same method, and **reproducible** if a different person or different equipment gives similar results. A repeat that is far from the others is an **anomalous result** and is normally left out of the mean.

bullets: **Acids (for example hydrochloric acid):** irritant to eyes and skin. **Control:** wear **eye protection** (goggles), wipe up spills, wash any splashes off skin with plenty of water.

**Alkalis (for example sodium hydroxide):** irritating to skin and eyes, and corrosive at higher concentrations. **Control:** goggles, use the lowest concentration that works, wash splashes immediately.
**Copper sulfate solution:** harmful if swallowed and harmful to the environment. **Control:** do not pour down the sink, dispose of waste as instructed and wash hands.
**Hydrogen gas (acid + metal):** extremely flammable. **Control:** no naked flames nearby and use small quantities of metal.
**Hot solutions:** large exothermic reactions can make the solution hot enough to burn. **Control:** use only the stated amounts and do not touch the cup.
**Glass thermometer or beaker:** can break and cause cuts. **Control:** do not use the thermometer as a stirrer, clamp or support firmly and sweep up breakages with a brush.
**Spilt liquid on the floor:** slip hazard. **Control:** mop up promptly.

**How to write a risk answer:** state the hazard, the harm it can do and the precaution (for example, ‘Hydrochloric acid is an irritant, so wear eye protection to prevent splashes damaging the eyes’).
core.h: Safety: hazards, risks and control measures
core.p: A **hazard** is something that could cause harm; a **risk** is the chance of harm happening; a **control measure** reduces the risk. You should be able to name a hazard from the chemicals or apparatus in the practical, say what harm it could cause, and suggest a sensible precaution. Eye protection is needed in every version of the practical. Chemicals such as hydrochloric acid and sodium hydroxide solution are irritants at the concentrations used in school (and the stronger the concentration, the higher the risk), while copper sulfate solution is harmful and harmful to the environment.

bullets: **Temperature change = final temperature − initial temperature.** A positive value means the temperature rose (exothermic); a negative value means it fell (endothermic).
**Example:** 21.0 °C to 27.5 °C gives a change of 27.5 − 21.0 = **+6.5 °C**.
**Mean of three repeats:** add the valid changes and divide by how many there are; ignore any anomalies first.
**Check:** the mean must lie between the smallest and largest valid values; if it does not, you have made an arithmetic error.
**Significant figures:** give the mean to the same number of decimal places as the raw data (or one more).
**Comparing conditions:** a bigger temperature change means more energy was transferred to the surroundings in that reaction (if the volume of solution is the same).
**Percentage difference or ratio (maths skill):** you may be asked to compare two means, for example ‘metal A gave a temperature rise twice as large as metal B’.
**Units:** temperature change is in degrees Celsius (°C); a change of 1 °C is the same size as a change of 1 K, but write °C in this practical.
core.h: Processing results: temperature change and mean
core.p: Raw readings are of limited use until you process them. First calculate the **temperature change** for each repeat by subtracting the starting temperature from the final temperature, keeping the sign so that you can tell exothermic (positive change) from endothermic (negative change). Then look for anomalies, calculate the **mean** of the valid temperature changes, and round sensibly. You should be able to do this calculation quickly and check that your answer lies within the range of the valid results.

bullets: **Axes:** independent variable on the x-axis, dependent on the y-axis, each labelled with the quantity and the unit (for example ‘Temperature (°C)’).

**Scale:** use more than half the grid in each direction, choose a scale that is easy to read (1, 2, 5 or 10 squares), and start the temperature axis at a suitable value (it does not have to start at zero).
**Plot points** accurately with small crosses or dots and check each one.
**Line of best fit:** a smooth line or a ruler line that passes close to as many points as possible, ignoring anomalies; it does not have to start at the origin.

**Neutralisation graph:** draw one line through the rising points and another through the falling points; where they intersect is the **end point** (maximum temperature and volume that exactly neutralises the acid).
**Why the temperature falls after the end point:** all the acid has reacted, so no more energy is released, and the excess alkali (which is cooler) cools the mixture.
**Reading values:** use the line of best fit to read the volume at the end point and the maximum temperature, and say how you used it.
**Gradient:** a steeper rising line means a faster rise in temperature per cm³ of alkali added; a flat line means no temperature change.
core.p: Graphs show patterns that a table of numbers hides. In this practical there are two common graphs. For a neutralisation, plot **temperature** (dependent variable) on the y-axis against **volume of alkali added** (independent variable) on the x-axis. The temperature rises as acid is neutralised, reaches a maximum when the acid and alkali have reacted completely (the **end point**), then falls as extra, cooler alkali is added with nothing left to react with. Draw **two straight lines of best fit** (one through the rising points, one through the falling points) and read the volume where they cross. For the cooling curve (temperature against time) the temperature rises quickly then falls slowly as energy is lost.

bullets: **Neutralisation (acid + alkali):** hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide → sodium chloride + water. Exothermic; temperature rises to a maximum at the end point.
**Displacement of metals:** zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper. Exothermic; the solution turns paler as blue copper ions are used up and a brown–pink solid of copper forms.
**Acid + metal:** magnesium + hydrochloric acid → magnesium chloride + hydrogen. Exothermic; bubbles of hydrogen are seen. The more reactive the metal, the bigger the temperature rise.
**Acid + carbonate:** sodium carbonate + acid → salt + water + carbon dioxide (effervescence).
**Endothermic example:** citric acid + sodium hydrogencarbonate. The temperature **falls**, so the change is negative.
**Dissolving some salts:** for example ammonium nitrate dissolving in water is endothermic and the temperature falls.
**What to compare:** metals (reactivity series), concentrations of acid, masses of reactant, or volumes of alkali added.
**Order of reactivity link:** a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one, and in general the bigger the difference in reactivity the larger the temperature rise.
core.p: Because the practical covers several reaction types, exam questions often give you one of them and ask you to plan or evaluate it. Each version has the same underlying method but different reagents, observations and hazards. Make sure you can write the symbol or word equation for each, say whether it is exothermic or endothermic, and identify the variable being investigated. A good answer links the temperature evidence to the energy transfer.

bullets: **Weakness:** energy transferred to the surroundings. **Effect:** the measured temperature rise is lower than the true value. **Improvement:** use a lid and extra insulation (a polystyrene cup inside a beaker).
**Weakness:** thermometer resolution of 1 °C. **Effect:** small temperature changes cannot be measured precisely. **Improvement:** use a digital probe reading to 0.1 °C.
**Weakness:** only one repeat. **Effect:** anomalies not spotted. **Improvement:** repeat three or more times and calculate a mean.
**Weakness:** the reaction is not complete before the reading is taken. **Improvement:** stir and wait for the temperature to stop changing, or use a data logger.
**Weakness:** uncontrolled variables such as different starting temperatures. **Improvement:** start every run at the same temperature.
**Writing a conclusion:** ‘As the volume of alkali increased up to 20 cm³ the temperature increased, so the reaction is exothermic’, with data quoted.
**Validity:** a test is valid if it only measures what it claims to, so controlling all other variables makes results valid.
**Further work:** repeat with other concentrations or other metals to see whether the pattern is general.
core.h: Evaluating the investigation and drawing conclusions
core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to judge how good the experiment was and how it could be improved. Always link a weakness to its effect on the results and then give a specific improvement. A **conclusion** must state the pattern shown by the data, use the data to support it, and be limited to what the experiment tested. You cannot conclude something about concentrations that you did not test, or about all metals if you only tested three.

bullets: **Link to energy changes:** the sign of the temperature change tells you whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic; the same idea is shown by reaction profiles.
**Link to neutralisation (4.4):** the end point of the temperature graph matches the point where acid and alkali react in the ratio shown by the balanced equation.

**Higher tier calculation:** if 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid is neutralised by 20 cm³ of sodium hydroxide, concentration of alkali = (1.0 × 25 ÷ 1000) ÷ (20 ÷ 1000) = 1.25 mol/dm³ (1:1 ratio).
**Link to reactivity series:** displacement reactions show how much more reactive a metal is than another through the size of the temperature rise.
**Command words:** ‘describe’ (give the method in order), ‘explain’ (give reasons using science), ‘evaluate’ (weigh strengths and weaknesses), ‘suggest’ (apply knowledge to a new situation).
**Mark allocation:** 6-mark method questions are level-marked, so include apparatus, quantities, measurements, controls, repeats and safety.
**Always include units** (°C, cm³, g) and state variables precisely, for example ‘the same volume (25 cm³) of acid’.
**Do not confuse** temperature with energy: temperature is a measure of how hot something is; energy transferred is what causes the change.
core.h: Links to other topics and exam skills
core.p: The temperature-change practical connects to many other parts of the specification. It supports 4.5.1.1 (exothermic and endothermic reactions), 4.5.1.2 (reaction profiles, where the sign of the overall energy change is shown), 4.4 (acids, bases and neutralisation, including titrations in the Higher tier), and 4.4.1 (the reactivity series for displacement reactions). It also practises working scientifically skills such as planning, variables, uncertainty, graph skills and evaluation, which are assessed throughout every paper.

exam: **Describe the method (6 marks):** write a logical sequence with quantities: measure a fixed volume of solution, record the start temperature, add the reagent, stir, record the highest temperature, repeat, and calculate the mean; include a safety point and one control variable for top level.
**Name equipment (1 mark):** polystyrene cup, lid, thermometer (or temperature probe), measuring cylinder, stirring rod; say why if asked.
**Temperature change (1–2 marks):** show ‘final − initial’ and give a sign and the unit °C.
**Mean (2 marks):** ignore anomalies, add valid values, divide by the number; show your working because method marks are available.
**Variables (2–3 marks):** name the independent, dependent and at least two control variables; say why controls matter in terms of fair testing.
**Explain why a lid and polystyrene cup are used (2 marks):** they are insulators, so less energy is transferred to the surroundings, and the temperature change measured is closer to the true value.
**Graph marks:** 1 for axes and labels with units, 1 for plotting, 1 for line(s) of best fit, 1 for reading values; read where lines intersect.
**Explain a graph shape (3 marks):** the temperature rises as acid is used up (exothermic), reaches a maximum when neutralisation is complete, then falls because excess cool alkali cools the mixture.
**Improve the experiment (2 marks):** state the improvement and its effect (for example a digital probe with higher resolution gives a more precise temperature change).
**Hazards (2 marks):** hazard + harm + control; for example ‘hydrochloric acid is an irritant – wear eye protection’.
**Conclusion (2–3 marks):** state the pattern, quote data, and say whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

mistakes.r: In an exothermic reaction the temperature rises because energy is transferred **to the surroundings** from the reacting chemicals.
mistakes.w: The temperature goes up because the reaction needs heat.

mistakes.r: Polystyrene is an **insulator**, so it reduces energy transfer to the surroundings and the measured temperature change is closer to the true value.
mistakes.w: A polystyrene cup is used because it is cheap and does not break.

mistakes.r: Repeats let you spot anomalies and calculate a **mean**, improving reliability; they do not remove a systematic error such as heat loss.
mistakes.w: Repeats make the results more accurate.

mistakes.r: Temperature change = **final − initial** = +6.5 °C; the sign shows whether the reaction is exothermic (+) or endothermic (−).
After the end point no more reaction occurs and the added alkali is cooler than the mixture, so the mixture cools.
mistakes.w: The temperature falls after the end point because the reaction becomes endothermic.

mistakes.r: Only change **one independent variable** at a time; keep the others as control variables so the test is valid.
mistakes.w: I will change the acid concentration and the volume of acid.

mistakes.r: Use a **stirring rod** and keep the thermometer still; glass thermometers can break if used as stirrers.
Wear eye protection to protect against **splashes of irritant or corrosive chemicals**; state the hazard and the harm.
mistakes.w: Wear eye protection because the solutions are hot.

mistakes.r: The lid reduces energy lost by evaporation and convection; it does not change the **rate** of reaction.
mistakes.w: The lid keeps the heat in so the reaction is faster.

summary: You must be able to carry out and evaluate the AQA required practical on temperature changes in reacting solutions (acid + metal, acid + carbonate, neutralisation and displacement), controlling variables, measuring the temperature change safely, processing results and drawing graphs. It matters because it is the practical evidence for exothermic and endothermic reactions and is examined in Paper 1, with its skills tested more widely.

terms.d: A reaction that transfers energy to the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings increases.
A reaction that takes in energy from the surroundings so the temperature of the surroundings decreases.
Final temperature minus initial temperature, measured in °C; positive for exothermic and negative for endothermic reactions.
The variable that is deliberately changed by the investigator.
The variable that is measured, which depends on the independent variable.
A variable that is kept the same so it does not affect the results.
A material that is a poor conductor of energy, such as polystyrene, which reduces energy transfer.
The smallest change in the quantity being measured that an instrument can detect.
Results are repeatable if the same investigator gets the same results using the same method and equipment.
Results are reproducible if a different investigator or different equipment and method give the same results.
A measurement is accurate if it is close to the true value.
Measurements are precise if repeated readings are close together with a small spread.
A result that does not fit the pattern of the other results, usually left out of the mean.
A reaction between an acid and an alkali (or base) that forms a salt and water; it is exothermic.
The point where the acid and alkali have exactly reacted; on the temperature graph it is the highest temperature.
A reaction in which a more reactive element takes the place of a less reactive element in a compound.
Something that has the potential to cause harm, such as an irritant chemical or hot liquid.
The chance that a hazard will cause harm, which can be reduced by control measures.
A line drawn on a graph that passes as close as possible to all the plotted points.
An error that affects every reading in the same direction, such as heat loss reducing every temperature rise.

worked.ans: Mean temperature change = +6.5 °C; the reaction is exothermic (anomaly: run 3).
worked.q: A student reacts zinc with copper sulfate solution three times. Starting and highest temperatures: (1) 21.0 → 27.5 °C; (2) 20.5 → 27.0 °C; (3) 21.0 → 31.0 °C. Calculate the mean temperature change, ignoring any anomalous result, and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic. (4 marks)
steps: Temperature change = final − initial for each run.
Run 3 (10.0 °C) is far from the other two, so it is **anomalous** and is ignored.
The temperature increased, so energy was transferred to the surroundings: **exothermic**.

worked.ans: (a) 20 cm³; (b) 14.0 °C; (c) all acid used up, no more energy released and cool excess alkali cools the mixture; (d) 1.25 mol/dm³.
worked.q: 25 cm³ of 1.0 mol/dm³ hydrochloric acid starts at 20.0 °C. Sodium hydroxide solution is added in 5 cm³ portions and the highest temperature after each portion is 23.5, 27.0, 30.5, 34.0, 33.0 and 32.0 °C (after 5, 10, 15, 20, 25 and 30 cm³). (a) What volume of alkali neutralises the acid? (b) What is the maximum temperature change? (c) Explain why the temperature falls after this volume. (d) Calculate the concentration of the sodium hydroxide (Higher tier). (6 marks)
steps: (a) The highest temperature, 34.0 °C, occurs after 20 cm³ so the end point is **20 cm³**.
(c) After 20 cm³ all the acid has reacted so no more energy is released; the extra alkali is cooler than the mixture, so the temperature falls.
(d) HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H2O, so the ratio is 1 : 1.
Moles HCl = 1.0 × 25 ÷ 1000 = 0.025 mol, so moles NaOH = 0.025 mol.

worked.ans: Model answer: Measure 25 cm³ of dilute HCl into a polystyrene cup in a beaker with a lid; record the start temperature; add 0.5 g of one metal, stir and record the highest temperature; calculate the change; repeat three times for a mean; repeat with the other metals keeping volume, concentration, mass, form and start temperature the same; wear goggles and avoid flames. The metal with the largest mean temperature change gives the biggest rise (and is the most reactive).
worked.q: Describe how you would investigate which of three metals (magnesium, zinc and iron) gives the largest temperature rise when added to dilute hydrochloric acid. (6 marks)
steps: Place a polystyrene cup in a beaker and add a lid, then use a measuring cylinder to measure 25 cm³ of dilute hydrochloric acid into the cup.
Record the starting temperature with a thermometer.
Weigh the same mass of metal (for example 0.5 g) in the same form for each metal, add it to the acid and replace the lid.
Stir gently and record the highest temperature reached.
Calculate the temperature change (final − initial); repeat at least three times and calculate a mean for each metal.
Keep the volume and concentration of acid, the mass and form of metal and the starting temperature constant.
Wear eye protection, keep flames away because hydrogen is produced.
